text: Matter A-1: Hartwell v. Telltale Cardiac Systems, Ashgrove County Superior Court, Case No. 25-CV-03817. Plaintiff Dorothea Hartwell filed her complaint on March 4, 2025. Kenge, Carboy & Vholes LLP defends Telltale Cardiac Systems; Walter Osgood is the partner and Priya Raghunathan the day-to-day associate. Plaintiff's counsel is Gideon Farrar.

Plaintiff alleges that the conductor coil of the ArcLine AL-4120 bipolar active-fixation pacing lead was unreasonably prone to fatigue fracture, that a safer alternative design was feasible, that Telltale knew of a heightened fracture rate before her implant, and that Telltale failed to warn implanting physicians of fracture risk near the clavicle and first rib. She demands compensatory damages above $1.9 million plus punitive damages.

The AL-4120 was implanted in Ms. Hartwell on March 19, 2019, at Westmarch Regional Hospital, through a subclavian approach. A routine interrogation on November 8, 2022, showed out-of-range impedance. The lead was revised surgically on November 15, 2022. Radiographs show the break about 4 cm from the pectoral pocket, in the segment that crosses beneath the clavicle.

Claimed damages: $214,000 in billed charges for the revision surgery and roughly $96,000 in lost earnings (Ms. Hartwell is a school administrator), plus general damages. The associate's memo of October 7, 2025 estimates realistic verdict exposure of $450,000 to $900,000 if liability is found, and fees and costs through trial of $410,000 to $520,000.

Telltale's complaint database shows 31 confirmed conductor fractures among about 22,000 AL-4120 leads shipped, a rate near 0.14 percent. The memo says engineering must still confirm that the rate stayed within the labeled range.

An engineer in the field circulated an internal note in 2020 saying returned leads showed wear from repeated bending near the pocket and suggesting the design be revisited. As of the October 2025 memo it had not been produced. The associate regards it as the most damaging undisclosed document.

A 2021 trend report followed an internal Telltale quality inquiry into returned-lead fractures, called the Larkspur review. As of the October 2025 memo, plaintiff had not asked about Larkspur by name. Plaintiff's regulatory witness is expected to say Telltale should have updated its warnings after the 2021 trend report.

The AL-4120 instructions for use warn against medial subclavian puncture and describe lateral venous access as the preferred approach. The operative note does not say which technique was used, and the memo calls that the most important open factual question.

Plaintiff's expected experts are Dr. Ruth Kellaway (biomedical engineer, who will say the coil pitch and insulation sleeve create a stress concentration), Dr. Leopold Quist (electrophysiologist, on causation), and a regulatory witness. Telltale's testifying design engineer is Dr. Henrik Vandermeer. As of the memo, Dr. Kellaway had not examined the explanted lead under magnification and had not ruled out subclavian crush from medial puncture.

The draft Answer, dated April 22, 2025 and marked as not yet filed and for partner review, admits that Telltale makes cardiac leads, that the AL-4120 was implanted on or about March 19, 2019, and (on information and belief) that the interrogation and revision occurred on November 8 and 15, 2022. It denies defect, inadequate warnings, and causation. It pleads lack of knowledge on plaintiff's residence, age, and damages.

Telltale's draft Answer pleads fifteen defenses. They include failure to state a claim, learned intermediary, adequate warnings, state of the art, regulatory compliance and preemption, no feasible safer alternative, causation, superseding cause, comparative fault, failure to mitigate, limitations and repose, misuse or alteration, setoff, and constitutional limits on punitive damages. The Answer also reserves the right to add defenses.

Learned intermediary defense: Telltale contends its duty to warn ran to the implanting physician, who was adequately warned through the instructions for use and related communications, and who exercised independent medical judgment. The memo says Dr. Anselm Teague's testimony drives both this defense and the causation challenge.

The draft Answer's own drafting notes flag three open points for the partner: whether to plead repose given the 2019 implant date, whether the client has signed off on the preemption language, and that the Eleventh Defense (limitations/repose) is a placeholder pending plaintiff's chart.
The firm's associate (October 2025 memo) recommends dropping the statute of repose defense from the final Answer because it is likely unavailable given the March 2019 implant date.

Discovery scope agreed by email in June 2025: Telltale will produce the AL-4120 design history file and the testing that supported its release. Complaint and returned-product analysis records for the AL-4120 run from first clinical use in 2018 through the November 15, 2022 revision date.

Telltale refuses to produce design files for the whole ArcLine family. It argues that models differ in coil pitch and insulation thickness and that a family-wide request is disproportionate in a single-model case. Mr. Farrar counters that Telltale's labeling treats ArcLine as one platform. He will consider limiting the request to the AL-4120 and its closest sibling only if given an engineering declaration on the differences.

Telltale agreed to send an informal engineering declaration limited to coil differences between the AL-4120 and the AL-4125, on the condition that it is not treated as a concession on family-wide relevance. The memo expects that declaration to hold the line on those two models against continued pressure for sibling-model files.

Telltale refused to produce post-revision events for leads returned from the implanting center, on the grounds that the request goes beyond Telltale's knowledge of its own product and implicates third-party patient information. Mr. Farrar had conditioned his agreement on the complaint window on receiving those events. The email thread does not record that dispute being resolved, and Ms. Raghunathan asked him to say if he intends to move on it.

Expert schedule agreed by email on June 19, 2025, subject to court approval of a stipulation: plaintiff's opening reports are due January 16, 2026, and Telltale's reports are due March 17, 2026. The parties agreed to sequential, not simultaneous, disclosure.

Counsel agreed that consulting experts are not discoverable and that draft expert reports and attorney–testifying-expert communications are protected, except for facts, data and assumptions counsel provided. Mr. Farrar was to send a stipulation, and Telltale was to circulate a draft protective order covering design and testing documents.

Dr. Anselm Teague, the treating cardiologist, was first noticed for deposition for the week of September 15, 2025. It slipped and was reset to November 6, 2025. Mr. Farrar refused to defer all expert depositions until after Dr. Teague testifies, citing uncertainty about his availability; Ms. Raghunathan said the expert deposition sequence would be revisited if he could not sit in the original window.
Dr. Teague is the only witness who can say whether lateral or medial access was used and what he understood from the instructions for use.

Strategy (memo): direct the first motion practice and first expert effort at Dr. Quist's and Dr. Kellaway's causation opinions rather than the design-defect debate. The aim is to test whether their opinion that the lead failed from design rather than placement is reliable and fits the facts. If a ruling limits Dr. Kellaway's causation opinion, the design theory loses its link to the injury. Only if that fails does Dr. Vandermeer meet the design theory directly. The associate rates summary judgment prospects as modest and trial prospects as good if causation is narrowed first.

Settlement posture (memo): Ms. Raghunathan has told plaintiff's counsel only that the firm cannot discuss numbers. Mr. Farrar has asked twice for a mediation date. The firm recommends declining until after the November 6, 2025 deposition and, if the transcript is favorable, proposing mediation in January 2026, with an authority request only after the deposition.

Firm plan for regulatory review (memo): Dr. Vandermeer to deliver a near-final draft by January 30, 2026, ahead of the March 17, 2026 deadline. Comments from the regulatory group must go through counsel, and what is sent must be logged so the exchange stays protected as work done at counsel's direction. The firm will confirm with Mr. Farrar that the draft-protection stipulation covers this process.

Industry-standards defense (memo): begin developing it now rather than waiting for Dr. Kellaway's reports, with a witness from the cardiac-device standards community explaining how standards for a lead like the AL-4120 are written and satisfied. That witness should be engaged separately from Dr. Vandermeer. Otherwise plaintiff could argue he is grading his own work, and a separate witness keeps him out of standards-committee questions.

Risks identified in the memo: (1) the missing operative detail on access technique, since medial puncture strengthens the defense and lateral access strengthens plaintiff's inherent-fatigue theory; (2) plaintiff arguing the 2021 trend report shows notice of a rising fracture rate; (3) Ms. Hartwell's credibility and sympathy after a hard recovery; (4) discovery creep on sibling-model files; (5) the likely unavailability of repose.

Next steps listed in the October 2025 memo: finalize the Dr. Teague deposition outline; get Dr. Vandermeer's CV and availability; outline a motion to exclude Dr. Quist's and Dr. Kellaway's opinions; and send Ms. Salvesen the November status note.

Delmore v. Telltale Cardiac Systems, No. 24-CV-01906, is pending in Linnet County Superior Court. Plaintiff Raymond Delmore sued over an ArcLine AL-4135 pacing lead. His First Amended Complaint was filed August 19, 2024 and pleads strict liability design defect (Count I), failure to warn (Count II) and negligence (Count III). Kenge, Carboy & Vholes LLP (Eleanor Haskett, partner; Tomas Brevik, associate) defends Telltale. Plaintiff's counsel is Ingrid Lowenthal.

Plaintiff alleges that the lead was implanted February 7, 2020 at Brannock Memorial Hospital (serial number ending 7731). Its insulation allegedly abraded at the suture sleeve, causing loss of capture in August 2023, a fall and a wrist fracture. The lead was later removed and replaced. Telltale admitted the implant and the August 2023 episode only on information and belief.

Plaintiff claims medical specials of $302,500 and about $410,000 in wage loss over a working life. He is a 54-year-old electrician who cannot return to full-duty work. His demand is $3.2 million. Brevik's July 2025 memo estimated realistic exposure at $600,000 to $1.4 million if liability is established, with roughly a 40% chance of an adverse liability finding.

The draft Answer (dated October 3, 2024, marked for E. Haskett's review and not for filing) denies the design-defect, failure-to-warn and negligence counts. It specifically denies that the insulation design caused abrasion at the suture sleeve, that Telltale knew of a pattern of such failures before February 2020, and that a feasible alternative design existed. It denies that the instructions for use were inadequate.

Telltale's draft Answer pleads 15 alternative defenses without accepting plaintiff's burdens. They include learned intermediary, adequate warnings, industry standards, regulatory approval and preemption, state of scientific knowledge, no safer feasible alternative, lack of causation, intervening cause, comparative fault, failure to mitigate, limitations, setoff and no basis for punitive damages.

Telltale's learned-intermediary defense says warnings went to the implanting physician, who made independent decisions on placement and fixation and whose practice would not have changed. Its causation defense says the fall and the loss of capture had other causes, including pre-existing conditions.

The draft Answer pleads that the risk was not known or knowable in 2020 and denies pre-2020 knowledge of a failure pattern. The July 2025 memo flags facts plaintiff may use against that. These are a cluster of eleven insulation-breach returns from one 2019 manufacturing period, and a 2019 polyurethane formula change by the supplier made without a formal change notice to Telltale. Telltale learned of the change only from a supplier email found in document collection.

The July 2025 memo says Delmore's lead serial number sits at the edge of the 2019 cluster range, and engineering had not yet determined whether the lead belongs to that manufacturing period. Lot membership is a listed top risk.

The AL-4135 passed the validation program that supported its release, and its field insulation-breach return rate was low overall. Telltale admits the lead was released for sale in 2018 after federal regulatory review.

Plaintiff's liability theory, per the July 2025 memo, is that the inner polyurethane layer creeps and abrades when a lead is anchored too tightly. His materials scientist is Dr. Samuel Achterberg and his electrophysiologist is Dr. Noreen Castellane. Telltale's design expert is Dr. Bertrand Ouellette, who believes the sleeve instructions were followed in design validation.

The key fact question is how tightly the suture sleeve was secured on February 7, 2020. The operative record is thin and the implanting surgeon will be a central witness. Plaintiff may also depose Josefina Strathmore, a former Telltale supplier-quality auditor who audited the insulation supplier in 2019.

The firm views causation as plaintiff's weak link. Loss of capture and a fall do not by themselves show insulation failure rather than a pre-existing conduction problem, and Delmore's records show a prior syncopal episode in 2021. The July 2025 memo plans to depose Dr. Castellane and evaluate a motion before spending time on the broader design issues.

The July 2025 memo recommends building the industry-standards defense now rather than waiting for expert disclosure. It proposes retaining Dr. Lucinda Marchetti, who served on the standard's lead-design working group, as a separate witness on the standard's origins and what compliance means. She would be kept apart from Dr. Ouellette to shield his design opinion from cross-examination about committee politics. The engagement would run through the firm, with a scope letter limited to the standard and its drafting history.

A protective order was entered November 12, 2024. It limits use of produced materials to this action. Telltale agreed to produce the 2019 design review minutes and the polyurethane supplier qualification file on a rolling basis, marked Confidential. Plaintiff's experts must sign the acknowledgment before receiving anything. Plaintiff's counsel said she will not share design documents with co-counsel on any other lead case.

Counsel agreed in March 2025 that transcript pages designated confidential are covered by the protective order, including attached exhibits and any summary quoting them. Before using designated material in a filing, the parties will meet and confer and file under seal if needed. Brevik proposed in his draft stipulation that the sealing procedure also apply to expert reports quoting designated documents.

The parties agreed on the scope of field-return production: insulation-breach returns for the AL-4135 and the AL-4130, from release in 2018 through the date of Delmore's lead removal. Plaintiff agreed not to pursue the rest of the ArcLine family. Plaintiff's rationale was that the AL-4130 shares the same insulation supplier.

Telltale initially objected to producing returns data for the full ArcLine family because other models have different insulation stacks. It agreed to include the AL-4130 only as a concession to avoid motion practice, and expressly not as an admission that the AL-4130 is relevant to plaintiff's claims.

Plaintiff's discovery priorities were the AL-4135 insulation design, internal abrasion analyses at suture sleeves, field-return data on insulation breaches, the 2019 design review minutes and the polyurethane supplier qualification file. Telltale committed to tell plaintiff by March 14, 2025 which internal abrasion analyses exist and which it would log as privileged.

The agreed expert schedule is plaintiff's opening reports on September 29, 2025, defense reports on October 31, 2025 and a single rebuttal round by December 5, 2025. Expert disclosures will include a six-year list of prior testimony, the fee schedule and materials considered. Telltale maintains that drafts and counsel communications stay protected except for facts, data and assumptions.
Lowenthal said she would send a stipulation memorializing the returns scope and the expert schedule. Brevik said his draft stipulation would add the sealing procedure for expert reports.

Client instruction on settlement: listen if plaintiff raises resolution, but do not respond with a number. Telltale will not put an offer on the table, in any form, until plaintiff's treating cardiologist has been deposed. After that deposition the firm must send the client an assessment and a recommended range. Authority above $500,000 requires approval by CFO Cormac Brightwater.

Lowenthal informally raised resolution talks on March 3, 2025, after the cardiologist's deposition. Brevik told her not to read anything into it. A confidential mediation with retired mediator Constance Aldrin is set for September 9, 2025. Plaintiff's counsel has indicated she will propose a figure around $2 million. Dr. Imogen Pratt, the cardiologist, is set to be deposed August 14, 2025.

The firm's July 2025 recommendation is to attend the mediation to listen and not put a number on the table unless Dr. Pratt's testimony helps. It will write to the client's general counsel, Marguerite Salvesen, immediately after the Pratt transcript arrives. The firm also flags that plaintiff may use the mediation to preview an aggressive punitive theory.

Telltale's expert reports are due October 31, 2025. Brevik asked Dr. Ouellette for a complete draft by September 26, 2025, leaving about five weeks before service. Dr. Marchetti's report, if served, would go through the same regulatory review, with drafts routed through counsel.

Okafor v. Toil & Trouble Home Products, Cause No. D-2026-1184, is pending in the District Court of Pelham Ridge County. Plaintiff Nkechi Okafor filed her Original Petition on February 17, 2026. Kenge, Carboy & Vholes LLP (partner Josephine Armitage, associate Marcus Teller) represents Toil & Trouble. Plaintiff's counsel is Leona Trevisan.

Plaintiff alleges that on December 14, 2025 the lid of her PressureMate TT-6200 (six-quart electric pressure cooker) rotated open while the unit was under pressure. She alleges second- and third-degree scald burns to her left forearm and upper chest. Her claims are design defect (the lid can be turned while pressurized) and negligence, including failure to test and failure to investigate prior complaints.

Plaintiff's claimed damages: medical charges of $87,500, two skin graft procedures, scarring, and about $38,000 in lost income as a dental hygienist. She demands $650,000 and also seeks exemplary damages. She is 38.

Plaintiff bought the unit on October 11, 2024 (the answer recites Marlowe Home & Hardware, $119.99, October 2024). Her counsel says it is from lot Q3-2024. Plaintiff says she was cooking dried beans, the pressure indicator was down, and the lid turned with ordinary effort and released a jet of hot liquid.

The draft answer (dated March 31, 2026, circulated for partner comment) pleads a general denial plus specific responses and defenses A–N. The defenses are: alteration or modification (gasket replacement, pin removal), misuse and failure to follow warnings, comparative responsibility, reservation of responsible-third-party designation, compliance with standards and independent lab safety listing, open and obvious risk, adequate warnings, no safer alternative design, no causation, failure to mitigate, limit on medical expenses to amounts paid or incurred, exemplary damages limits, credit/offset, and preservation with an adverse-inference demand.

Toil & Trouble's pleaded position is that the unit was not in the same condition as when it left its control. It also says it has not inspected the unit and demands that it be preserved. It lacks knowledge of the incident, the injuries and the purchase, and so denies them. It denies that a feasible alternative design, such as a secondary mechanical lockout, existed.

Client records show a replacement gasket was sent in July 2025 to a household at Ms. Okafor's address. The client's general counsel flagged this early as possibly important, and the memo treats it as raising an alteration question. The memo also notes it cuts both ways: if Toil & Trouble sent the part, plaintiff will say it sent the wrong one. The July 2025 gasket shipment records still need to be pulled.

A retail employee told the client's investigator that the box for this unit had been returned once and resold as new. If true, this could undercut Ms. Okafor's account that she bought it new. The client also asked to learn whether the unit was bought new from the retailer or through another channel.

Plaintiff's likely experts: Dr. Gareth Pellam, a mechanical engineer, who will probably say the lockout pin can stick when coated with starch or foam from beans, letting the ring turn under pressure. Dr. Yvette Hargrove, a human-factors witness, will address the manual's warnings. The memo assumes both will be designated.

Firm strategy on experts: attack Dr. Pellam's causation opinion first, before engaging on whether a different lid mechanism would be a better design. The questions are whether his sticking-pin opinion rests on testing and fits the facts (ordinary-use scenario, replacement gasket, pin condition on inspection), whether he replicated the failure on a comparable unit, and whether he ruled out a gasket problem. If he did not, challenge his reliability. A narrowed causation case makes the alternative-design argument less relevant.

The client's instruction is to try mediation before any testifying experts are disclosed or deposed, because expert discovery is expensive and hardens positions. Consulting engineers may attend the inspection. If plaintiff's counsel pressed for an expert schedule first, the firm was to insist on a mediation date and tell the client if she objected.

Agreed schedule (emails of April 20 to May 1, 2026): mediation by July 17, 2026. If the case does not settle, plaintiff designates experts August 21, defense October 2, and expert depositions follow in November. Leona Trevisan was to draft the scheduling order. Her conditions for accepting mediation were pre-mediation production and fixed expert dates.

Agreed discovery terms: Toil & Trouble will produce the lid design file, the test reports supporting the safety listing, and the complaint reports by June 5, 2026. Complaints cover lid-related incidents on the TT-6200 from the 2023 launch through December 14, 2025. TT-5500 complaints are included only where the report describes the pin as the failing element. Other models are excluded as having a different lid design. Lot data is limited to line inspection records for the week of manufacture of the Q3-2024 lot units, not the whole quarter.

Only testifying experts will be deposed, and neither side will disclose non-testifying consultants. Anyone who touches the unit will be named in the inspection protocol. Marcus proposed a cap of 25 interrogatories per side, including subparts, until mediation is done. He also proposed that depositions of Ms. Okafor and Toil & Trouble's product safety lead may occur before mediation, with other fact depositions held until afterward. Plaintiff's response to those two proposals is not in the documents.

Inspection: plaintiff's counsel has the unit secured at her consulting engineer's lab, and a joint non-destructive inspection was agreed. The protocol covers photographs, measurement of the locking ring and lockout pin, and no disassembly until both sides' engineers agree on steps. The firm sent the draft protocol on April 24, 2026. The client instructed that nothing be disassembled or cleaned before both engineers are present, and that its own engineer handle the unit only in the lawyer's presence.

The firm wants the inspection finished by the end of June 2026. Dr. Oswin Takahashi, the defense engineer, should attend and give a preliminary read, not a formal report, before mediation. Items to preserve: the pin's travel, residue on the pin and seat, the gasket's origin, and the state of the ring.

Mediator: plaintiff's counsel suggested retired trial judge Harlan Whitcombe, who has handled product cases. Marcus said he was acceptable in principle, subject to the client's confirmation. The memo recommends him. Client confirmation and preliminary mediation authority were still to be obtained.

Preliminary exposure assessment (memo of May 12, 2026): likely range of $140,000 to $320,000, with a midpoint of $230,000 and a modest chance of a defense verdict. The memo says liability is unlikely to be a landslide, but a scarred, sympathetic plaintiff and a pressure-hazard consumer product is a hard combination before a jury. The view is preliminary because the unit has not been inspected.

Risks identified in the memo: residue on the pin consistent with bean foam would strengthen Dr. Pellam's theory; the three complaints may be characterized as notice; the replacement gasket cuts both ways; damages include two grafts and visible scarring; spoliation exposure (see the preservation item).

Preservation: the firm must confirm the unit was preserved since the December 2025 incident. Ms. Trevisan says it has been in a lab since February. The client issued a litigation hold on February 26, 2026. The client also asked the firm to have the retailer, Marlowe Home & Hardware, preserve its sales records for the unit.

Estate of Sven Lindqvist v. Joad Axle Works, Tamarack County Superior Court No. TC-23-0459, is a wrongful death action filed May 30, 2023 by Karin Lindqvist as personal representative. Our client Joad Axle Works is the defendant. Kenge, Carboy & Vholes represents Joad: Cornelius Vandeleur is the partner and Imani Rutherford the associate.

On June 9, 2022, Sven Lindqvist, 47, was driving a Redfern Freight tractor-trailer down the State Route 114 exit ramp when it rolled onto its side. He died at the scene. The left spindle of the JX-9 tandem drive axle was found separated at the inboard bearing shoulder.

The Estate alleges that the spindle fractured first and caused the loss of control. It attributes this to an inadequate fillet radius and heat treatment and to inadequate pre-release fatigue testing. It also pleads failure to warn, claims economic loss above $2.4 million, demands $11.5 million and pleads punitive damages.

The draft Answer is dated July 14, 2023 and was marked for partner review before filing. Joad admits it made the JX-9 assembly, sold in 2018 to a tractor builder and later installed in a tractor operated by Redfern Freight. It denies selling to the decedent or to Redfern directly. It admits, on information and belief, that the left spindle was found separated near the inboard bearing shoulder.

The draft Answer denies that the JX-9 was defectively designed or manufactured. It also denies that the spindle separation preceded and caused the loss of control, and denies that any act or omission of Joad caused the rollover.

The draft Answer pleads fifteen defenses, including: no defect; industry standards and state of the art; post-sale alteration; inadequate maintenance; superseding cause; comparative fault (speed, hours of service, no pre-trip inspection); several-only apportionment; causation (post-rollover impact may explain the spindle's condition); adequate warnings; limitations and repose; setoff; no basis for punitive damages; and a preservation demand with a request for a joint inspection protocol.

The draft Answer pleads lack of knowledge about the route, speed, load and driving conduct on June 9, 2022. The January 2024 memo reports an electronic data recorder reading of 41 mph on a ramp posted at 35 mph. Anyone relying on the Answer should confirm whether it was amended or filed as drafted, given the speed evidence.

The sequence question, whether the spindle failed before the rollover or in it, is genuinely contested and may decide the case. Plaintiff's metallurgist, Dr. Fenwick Ashdown, will argue that beach marks show months of fatigue progression and that the spindle was cracked before June 9.

Joad's own metallurgist's preliminary read is that the final overload zone is large and the fracture surface shows heavy smearing from post-separation contact, which is consistent with an impact failure.

Joad has a privileged post-accident metallurgical review that found a machining tool mark at the fracture origin. The reviewer could not rule it out as the initiation point. The report has not been produced and is being withheld as work product. It is a sensitive adverse fact on the sequence question.

Plaintiff's reconstructionist, Dr. Lorraine Pettibone, will say the ramp speed was within the legal limit and that the driver had no reasonable explanation for the loss of control except axle failure. Our counter is the recorder's 41 mph reading on a 35 mph ramp, which supports comparative fault and an alternative cause.

Joad's fatigue series FT-77, run in 2017, is central to discovery. Four specimens reached runout and one failed at 82 percent of runout, which plaintiff will use to argue an inadequate safety margin. Joad's chief axle engineer, Bertil Oakhurst, ran the 2017 test program and will be a central witness. Hollis Pruett, a former Joad test technician who left in 2019 and carried out the FT-77 testing, may be deposed by plaintiff.

Client instruction, followed by the firm: Joad will not stipulate to the authenticity of its internal test data (including the 2017 fatigue series) until a protective order is in place, and it requires an outside-counsel-and-experts-only tier. It will produce only what the court requires, and not before the order is signed. The firm told plaintiff's counsel this on October 9, 2023.

The firm recommends holding the line on any blanket authenticity stipulation, because the test data will be a core part of plaintiff's affirmative case. After the protective order is signed, authenticity can be discussed document by document.

Plaintiff's counsel, Octavia Brandvold, asked for design drawings, heat-treatment specifications, fatigue and bench test data, warranty and failure reports, and builder communications. In October 2023 she agreed to an attorneys'-eyes-only tier for the test data. She said she would sign the protective order if that tier covers the FT-77 data and the design drawings. The firm's draft order, sent October 17, 2023, has both tiers. Joad also asked that the order bar use of produced material outside this case and require return or destruction at the end.

Discovery scope was negotiated down. Joad refused warranty and failure reports for the entire JX line, because the JX-9 spindle is a distinct forging and the JX-7 and JX-11 have different spindle geometry. The parties agreed on JX-9 spindle reports from 2018 through June 9, 2022, plus JX-9 wheel-end bearing-shoulder reports. Plaintiff will not seek JX-7 or JX-11 data unless discovery shows the JX-9 spindle shares a part with them.

Agreed expert schedule (October 2023 emails): plaintiff's reports March 8, 2024; defense reports June 14, 2024 (about 98 days later); plaintiff's rebuttal July 8, 2024. Joad had asked for July 8 for defense reports. Each side will list the materials its experts considered.

Both sides plan to subpoena Redfern Freight's maintenance records for the tractor, including the last three bearing services, and to share what comes back. Joad also asked whether the Estate plans to depose Joad's chief axle engineer before the expert reports are due. If so, Joad wants that deposition after the bearing-shoulder reports are produced.

Strategy recommended in the memo: build the industry-standards defense early, and retain Dr. Mathilde Grosvenor, who chairs the relevant standards subcommittee, as a separate witness on what the standards require. Dr. Raul Esquivel would address this axle's design and testing. Keeping them separate avoids one expert vouching for both the design and the yardstick, and shields Dr. Esquivel from cross-examination on committee matters. Dr. Grosvenor's retention letter should be limited to the standards and their history.

Strategy recommended in the memo: challenge plaintiff's causation expert first. The questions are whether the opinion that the spindle was cracked before June 9 rests on any testing or replication, whether it rules out separation during the rollover and the 41 mph reading, and what the smeared spindle shows after eight months in a yard. If causation is narrowed, the fillet-radius and heat-treatment arguments matter far less.

The memo does not recommend settlement talks now, because the sequence evidence is too uncertain and the Estate would price the case on the worst version of the test data. After the spindle examination, if the sequence picture is favorable, a number in the $1.2 million to $2 million range could be explored. The upper part of that range would need the board process, so it must be flagged early. The Estate has made no formal demand beyond the complaint figure.

The January 22, 2024 memo assesses this as the most serious exposure in the docket for Joad. It estimates a gross verdict range of $3.5 million to $7 million if liability is established, with about a 35 percent probability of an adverse liability finding. It projects fees and costs through trial of $780,000 to $960,000; the client expected $700,000 to $1,000,000.

Risks listed in the memo: the FT-77 specimen that failed short of runout; jury sympathy (a widow with two teenage children); the Redfern maintenance records (a missed bearing service helps the alteration and maintenance defenses, but plaintiff may blame Joad's manual); spoliation and chain of custody, since the spindle sat eight months in a yard before it was moved; and the punitive claim, which alleges no specific facts.

Preservation: Joad issued a litigation hold to its departments on June 15, 2023. The client asked the firm for its own preservation recommendations, especially for the 2017 test lab. The fractured spindle and the tractor are in a storage facility not under Joad's control.

Confidential background: Joad changed its spindle forging supplier in 2020 after an internal audit. The client asked that the reason not be discussed with anyone outside the case team. Its supplier-qualification program is called Corbelmark, and the firm should understand how it works before any supplier discussion.
